name: Python
description: Semantics, the data model, idioms and the gotchas that bite in interviews and production.

modules.name: The Big Picture
modules.description: What Python is, what it is for, and the words everything else builds on.

cards.prompt: What is Python, and what is it mainly used for?
cards.answer: A general-purpose, high-level language built for readability. It dominates data science and machine learning, and is widely used for scripting and automation, web back ends (Django, Flask, FastAPI), testing and teaching.
cards.explanation: Python trades raw speed for how quickly people can write and read it. Where speed matters, the heavy lifting is done by libraries written in C, C++ or Rust (NumPy, PyTorch, Polars) that Python code drives — which is why a "slow" language runs most of the world's machine learning.

cards.prompt: Who created Python, and what idea shaped its design?
cards.answer: Guido van Rossum, first released in 1991. Its guiding idea is that code is read far more often than it is written, so it favours clear, uncluttered syntax — indentation instead of braces, and "one obvious way to do it".
cards.explanation: The informal design principles are collected in "The Zen of Python" (PEP 20): run `import this` to print them. "Readability counts" and "Explicit is better than implicit" are the two lines you will hear quoted most often in code reviews.

cards.prompt: How does Python code get from a `.py` file to a running program?
cards.answer: You run it with an interpreter: `python script.py`. The standard interpreter, CPython, first compiles the source to bytecode, then executes that bytecode on its virtual machine. There is no separate build step.
cards.explanation: Because there is no ahead-of-time compile, Python finds many mistakes only when the offending line actually runs. That is the trade for its fast edit-run loop — and why tests, linters and type checkers matter so much in Python projects. The interactive REPL (`python` with no arguments) runs code one line at a time.

resources.title: Python docs — Using the Python interpreter

cards.prompt: What does a minimal Python program look like?
cards.code: print("Hello, world!")
cards.answer: A single line. No class, no `main` function and no semicolons are required — top-level statements just run, in order.
cards.explanation: `print` is a built-in function that writes to standard output. Python uses indentation to group statements (blocks), so whitespace is part of the syntax; most other languages use braces for that.

cards.prompt: What kind of language is Python: typing, memory and paradigms?
cards.answer: Dynamically typed (types belong to values, checked at run time) but strongly typed (no silent `"1" + 1`). Memory is managed automatically by reference counting plus a cycle-detecting garbage collector. It is multi-paradigm: procedural, object-oriented and functional styles all work.
cards.explanation: Optional type hints (`def f(x: int) -> str`) can be checked by tools such as mypy or pyright, but the interpreter ignores them at run time. "Everything is an object" — numbers, functions and classes included — is the model that explains most of the language's behaviour.

cards.prompt: How do you install third-party libraries in Python, and what is a virtual environment?
cards.answer: Packages come from PyPI (the Python Package Index) and are installed with `pip` (or the faster `uv`). A virtual environment (`python -m venv .venv`) is a per-project folder of installed packages, so two projects can depend on different versions without clashing.
cards.explanation: Installing everything into the system Python leads to version conflicts and can break OS tools that rely on it. The habit to build from day one: one virtual environment per project, with dependencies recorded in `pyproject.toml` (or `requirements.txt`).

resources.title: Python Packaging User Guide — Installing packages

modules.name: Core Semantics
modules.description: Names, binding, scope and the rules that explain most surprising Python behaviour.

cards.prompt: In Python, what does assignment (`x = y`) actually do?
cards.answer: It binds the **name** `x` to the same object `y` refers to. It never copies the object.
cards.explanation: Python has names and objects, not boxes holding values. Assignment rebinds a name in a namespace; the object is untouched. This single rule explains aliasing, mutable default arguments, and why `a = b` on a list means both names see the same list.

resources.title: Python docs — Execution model: naming and binding

cards.prompt: What does this print?
cards.code:
def add(item, bucket=[]):
    bucket.append(item)
    return bucket

print(add(1))
print(add(2))
cards.explanation: Default arguments are evaluated **once**, when the `def` statement executes — not per call. The same list object is reused on every call that omits the argument. The fix is `bucket=None` plus `if bucket is None: bucket = []`.

cards.prompt: What does this print?
cards.code:
fns = [lambda: i for i in range(3)]
print([f() for f in fns])
cards.explanation: Closures capture the **variable**, not its value at creation time. By the time the lambdas run, the comprehension has finished and `i` is 2. Bind eagerly with a default argument — `lambda i=i: i` — to capture the current value.

resources.title: Python FAQ — Why do lambdas defined in a loop with different values all return the same result?

cards.prompt: `is` vs `==`
cards.answer: `is` compares identity (same object); `==` compares value via `__eq__`.

points: Correct for values: numbers, strings, containers

cards.explanation: Use `is` only for singletons. `x is 1000` may be False while `x == 1000` is True, because CPython interns only small integers (-5..256) and some strings. Never rely on interning for correctness.

cards.prompt: Python resolves names in the order Local → ___ → Global → Builtins.
cards.answer: Enclosing
cards.explanation: The LEGB rule: Local (current function), Enclosing (any outer function), Global (module), Builtins. `global` rebinds at module level; `nonlocal` rebinds in the nearest enclosing function scope.

cards.prompt: Which values are falsy in Python?
cards.answer: `False`, `None`, zero of any numeric type, and empty containers/strings — plus any object whose `__bool__` returns False or whose `__len__` returns 0.
cards.explanation: `if x:` calls `bool(x)`, which tries `__bool__` then `__len__`, defaulting to True. That is why `if my_list:` is idiomatic for 'not empty', but `if x is not None:` is required when 0 or an empty list are legitimate values.

cards.prompt: What does this print?
cards.code:
a = [1, 2, 3]
b = a
b.append(4)
print(a, b, a is b)
cards.explanation: `b = a` binds a second name to the same list. Mutating through either name is visible through both. Copy explicitly with `a[:]`, `list(a)` or `copy.deepcopy` when you need independence.

cards.prompt: What do `*args` and `**kwargs` mean in a signature, and what do `*` and `/` mean on their own?
cards.answer: `*args` collects extra positionals into a tuple, `**kwargs` collects extra keywords into a dict. A bare `*` forces everything after it to be keyword-only; a bare `/` forces everything before it to be positional-only.
cards.explanation: Positional-only (`/`, PEP 570) lets you rename parameters without breaking callers. Keyword-only (`*`, PEP 3102) stops callers passing booleans and flags as unlabelled positionals, which is the single cheapest readability win in an API.

modules.name: Data Model & Objects
modules.description: Dunder methods, classes, descriptors and how Python objects really behave.

cards.prompt: What is the Python data model, and why do dunder methods matter?
cards.answer: It is the set of protocols (`__len__`, `__iter__`, `__getitem__`, `__eq__`, `__enter__`…) that built-in syntax and functions dispatch to. Implementing them makes your object work with `len()`, `for`, `in`, `with`, operators and unpacking.
cards.explanation: Python's syntax is a thin veneer over the data model: `len(x)` is `type(x).__len__(x)`, `a + b` is `type(a).__add__`, `with x:` is `__enter__`/`__exit__`. Building on those protocols is what makes a class feel native rather than bolted on.

resources.title: Fluent Python (Ramalho) — the Python data model

cards.prompt: What does this print?
cards.answer:
B
['D', 'B', 'C', 'A', 'object']
cards.explanation: Python linearises multiple inheritance with C3: depth-first, left-to-right, but a class never precedes its subclasses. `D.__mro__` is the exact lookup order, and `super()` walks it — which is why cooperative `super()` calls in every class matter with diamonds.

resources.title: Python docs — The Python 2.3 method resolution order

cards.prompt: What does `__slots__` do?
cards.answer: It replaces the per-instance `__dict__` with a fixed array of descriptors — cutting memory per instance substantially and blocking new attributes at runtime.
cards.explanation: A normal instance carries a dict (tens of bytes of overhead plus hashing). `__slots__ = ('x', 'y')` stores attributes in a compact struct instead. The trade-offs: no dynamic attributes, no default `__weakref__` unless declared, and inheritance rules get fiddly.

cards.prompt: `@dataclass` vs `NamedTuple`
cards.answer: Dataclasses are mutable, flexible classes; NamedTuples are immutable tuples with names.

right.title: NamedTuple
points: Is a real tuple — unpacks and indexes
Awkward to extend or add behaviour

cards.explanation: Reach for a NamedTuple for small immutable value records that flow through tuple-shaped APIs; a dataclass for anything with behaviour, defaults or mutation. `frozen=True, slots=True` dataclasses get you close to the best of both.

cards.prompt: You need a resource released even when the body raises. What is the idiomatic Python mechanism, and how do you write one?
cards.answer: A context manager: implement `__enter__`/`__exit__`, or decorate a generator with `@contextlib.contextmanager` and put the cleanup in a `finally`.
cards.explanation: `with` guarantees `__exit__` runs on normal exit, exception, `return` and `break`. Returning True from `__exit__` swallows the exception — almost always wrong unless you mean it. `contextlib.ExitStack` composes an unknown number of them at runtime.

cards.prompt: What does this print?
cards.code:
def gen():
    print('start')
    yield 1
    print('middle')
    yield 2

g = gen()
print('created')
print(next(g))
print(next(g))
cards.answer:
created
start
1
middle
2
cards.explanation: Calling a generator function runs **no** body code — it builds a generator object. The body advances only on each `next()`, up to and including the next `yield`. That laziness is what makes generators memory-flat over huge sequences.

cards.prompt: This decorator works, but something important is lost. What, and how do you fix it?
cards.answer: The wrapper replaces the function's metadata: `add.__name__` is now `'wrapper'` and the docstring is gone. Fix it with `@functools.wraps(fn)` on `wrapper`.
cards.explanation: `functools.wraps` copies `__name__`, `__doc__`, `__module__`, `__qualname__` and `__dict__`, and sets `__wrapped__` so `inspect.signature` can see through the decorator. Without it, introspection, docs tooling and debuggers all lie about your function.

cards.prompt: If you define `__eq__` on a class, what happens to hashing, and what is the contract?
cards.answer: Defining `__eq__` sets `__hash__` to None, making instances unhashable. The contract: equal objects must have equal hashes, and a hash must not change while the object is in a container.
cards.explanation: Python removes the inherited identity hash because it would break the invariant. Either define `__hash__` over the same immutable fields you compare, or use `@dataclass(frozen=True)`, which generates a matching pair for you.

modules.name: Runtime, Async & Performance
modules.description: The GIL, concurrency choices, memory behaviour and where Python time actually goes.

cards.prompt: What is the GIL, and what does it actually prevent?
cards.answer: The Global Interpreter Lock lets only one thread execute Python bytecode at a time in a CPython process. It prevents CPU-bound parallelism across threads — not concurrency, and not parallel I/O.
cards.explanation: Threads still help for I/O: the GIL is released around blocking syscalls and in many C extensions (NumPy, compression, hashing). For CPU-bound work use `multiprocessing`, a C extension that releases the GIL, or the free-threaded build (PEP 703) where available.

cards.prompt: You must fetch 5,000 HTTP endpoints, then run an expensive pure-Python transform on each response. How do you structure the concurrency?
cards.answer: `asyncio` (or a thread pool) for the I/O fan-out, then hand the CPU-bound transform to a `ProcessPoolExecutor`.
cards.explanation: I/O waits release the GIL, so thousands of sockets are cheap with async or threads. The transform is bytecode-bound, so it needs separate processes to use more than one core. `loop.run_in_executor` with a process pool bridges the two halves cleanly.

cards.prompt: This async handler serves one request at a time. Why?
cards.code:
import asyncio, time

async def handle(n):
    time.sleep(1)          # simulate work
    return n * 2

async def main():
    await asyncio.gather(*(handle(i) for i in range(10)))
cards.answer: `time.sleep` blocks the event loop thread, so nothing else can run. Use `await asyncio.sleep(1)`, or push genuinely blocking work to `asyncio.to_thread` / an executor.
cards.explanation: An event loop is cooperative: a coroutine holds the thread until it awaits. Any synchronous blocking call — `time.sleep`, `requests.get`, heavy CPU loops, blocking DB drivers — stalls every other task on that loop.

cards.prompt: List comprehension vs generator expression
cards.answer: `[...]` materialises every element; `(...)` yields them one at a time.

left.title: [x for x in it]
points: Allocates the whole list up front
Faster when you need every element twice

cards.explanation: `sum(x*x for x in range(10**8))` runs in constant memory; the list version tries to allocate gigabytes. Prefer generators for pipelines and single passes, lists when you need random access or multiple traversals.

cards.prompt: Average-case complexity of `d[key]`, `d[key] = v` and `key in d` on a Python dict?
cards.answer: All O(1) on average; O(n) in the pathological collision case.
cards.explanation: CPython dicts are open-addressed hash tables; since 3.6 they use a compact layout (a sparse index array pointing into a dense entries array) that also preserves insertion order, guaranteed by the language from 3.7. Worst case only appears with adversarial or degenerate hashes; string hashing is randomised per process to defend against that.

cards.prompt: Why is this quadratic, and what is the fix?
cards.answer: Strings are immutable, so each `+=` allocates and copies the whole accumulated string — O(n²) total. Use `','.join(parts)` or accumulate into a list and join once.
cards.explanation: CPython has an in-place optimisation when a string has a refcount of one, so this sometimes looks fast — but it is not guaranteed and disappears the moment another name references `out`. `join` computes the final size once and copies each part exactly once.

cards.prompt: Two things are wrong with this error handling. What are they?
cards.answer: A bare `except:` also swallows `KeyboardInterrupt` and `SystemExit`, and the original traceback is discarded. Catch `Exception` (or the specific type) and log with `logging.exception` or re-raise with `raise ... from err`.
cards.explanation: Bare except catches everything deriving from `BaseException`, so Ctrl-C stops working. Losing the traceback turns a five-minute debug into an afternoon. If you truly cannot handle it, do not catch it.

cards.prompt: In modern Python, `Optional[int]` is written more plainly as `int | ___`.
cards.answer: None
cards.explanation: PEP 604 added the `X | Y` union syntax (Python 3.10+), so `Optional[int]` is `int | None` and `Union[str, bytes]` is `str | bytes`. Type hints are not enforced at runtime — they exist for readers, editors and static checkers such as mypy or pyright.

resources.title: PEP 604 — Allow writing union types as X | Y

modules.name: Everyday Idioms
modules.description: Comprehensions, slicing, unpacking, iteration helpers and the idioms that make code Pythonic.

cards.prompt: What does this print?
cards.code:
print([x * x for x in range(5) if x % 2 == 0])
print({k: v for k, v in [('a', 1), ('b', 2)]})
print({n % 3 for n in [1, 4, 5]})
cards.explanation: List, dict and set comprehensions share one shape: `expr for x in iterable if cond`. They build the whole collection eagerly and have their own scope, so the loop variable does not leak. Prefer them over `map`/`filter` with lambdas; switch to a plain loop once there is more than one condition or a side effect.

cards.prompt: What does this print?
cards.explanation: `seq[start:stop:step]` — start is inclusive, stop exclusive, and negative indices count from the end. A negative step walks backwards, so `[::-1]` reverses. Slicing a list always returns a new (shallow) list, which is why `a[:]` is a copy idiom. Out-of-range slice bounds are clamped rather than raising.

cards.prompt: What does this print?
cards.code:
first, *middle, last = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
print(first, middle, last)
a, b = 1, 2
a, b = b, a
print(a, b)
cards.explanation: Extended unpacking (PEP 3132) lets one starred target absorb "the rest" as a list. The right-hand side is evaluated fully before any assignment, which is why `a, b = b, a` swaps without a temporary. Unpacking works on any iterable and raises `ValueError` if the counts do not match.

cards.prompt: This works, but it is not idiomatic and has a latent bug. What would you write instead?
cards.code:
for i in range(len(names)):
    print(i, names[i], scores[i])
cards.answer: Iterate directly: `for i, (name, score) in enumerate(zip(names, scores)):`. Index loops are noisy, and if the lists differ in length this raises `IndexError` — while plain `zip` silently truncates. Use `zip(names, scores, strict=True)` (3.10+) to make a length mismatch an error.
cards.explanation: `enumerate` gives the index and the item together; `zip` walks several iterables in lockstep. Both are lazy, so they work on generators and files too. `strict=True` turns the silent truncation — a classic data-loss bug when two lists drift apart — into a loud `ValueError`.

cards.prompt: What can go inside an f-string, and what do `!r`, `:>10` and `=` do?
cards.answer: Any expression. `!r` uses `repr()` instead of `str()`, a format spec after `:` controls layout (`:>10` right-aligns in 10 columns, `:.2f` two decimals, `:,` thousands separators), and a trailing `=` (3.8+) prints the expression text as well as its value — `f"{x=}"` gives `x=42`.
cards.explanation: f-strings are evaluated at runtime and are the fastest and clearest formatting option. Do not use them to build SQL, shell commands or log messages: parameterise queries, pass argument lists to subprocess, and give logging a format string plus arguments so formatting is skipped for disabled levels.

cards.prompt: The assignment expression operator `:=`, which assigns and returns a value inside an expression, is nicknamed the ___ operator.
cards.answer: walrus
cards.explanation: PEP 572 (3.8) added it for cases like `while (chunk := f.read(8192)):` or `if (m := pattern.match(s)):` — computing a value once and testing it in the same expression. It is deliberately not allowed as a bare statement; outside those loop-and-test shapes, a normal assignment on its own line is clearer.

cards.prompt: What does structural pattern matching (`match`/`case`) add beyond a switch statement?
cards.answer: It destructures: patterns match on shape and type and bind names in one step — sequences (`[x, y, *rest]`), mappings (`{"type": "click", "pos": (x, y)}`), class patterns (`Point(x=0, y=y)`), alternatives with `|`, and guards with `if`.
cards.explanation: The trap: a bare name in a pattern is a capture, not a comparison — `case RED:` binds anything to `RED`. Compare against constants with dotted names (`Color.RED`) or literals. `case _:` is the wildcard default. It shines for parsing commands, ASTs and JSON-like messages.

cards.prompt: EAFP vs LBYL
cards.answer: EAFP — "easier to ask forgiveness than permission" — tries the operation and catches the failure; LBYL — "look before you leap" — checks first. Python idiom favours EAFP.

right.title: LBYL (check first)
points: Race-prone for files, locks, shared state

cards.explanation: EAFP is not just style: `if os.path.exists(p): open(p)` has a time-of-check-to-time-of-use race, while `try: open(p)` does not. Keep the `try` block tiny so you only catch the failure you expected, and use LBYL where the check is cheap and failure is the common case.

cards.prompt: What does this print?
cards.code:
print(sorted(['bo', 'dee', 'al', 'cy'], key=len))
print(sorted([('c', 2), ('b', 1), ('a', 2)], key=lambda p: (p[1], p[0])))
cards.explanation: `sorted` takes a `key` function computed once per element, and Timsort is stable — equal keys keep their input order, so `bo` stays ahead of `al`. Sort by several fields with a tuple key, or in successive passes from least to most significant. `sort()` sorts in place and returns `None`, a frequent source of `NoneType` errors.

cards.prompt: What does this print?
cards.explanation: `//` floors toward negative infinity (so `-7 // 2` is -4, not -3 as in C or Java truncation) and `%` takes the sign of the divisor so that `(a // b) * b + a % b == a` always holds. `/` always returns a float. Python ints are arbitrary precision, so they never overflow — they just get slower as they grow.

cards.prompt: What does this print?
cards.code:
import copy
a = [[1], [2]]
shallow = copy.copy(a)
deep = copy.deepcopy(a)
shallow[0].append(99)
print(a, deep)
cards.explanation: `copy.copy` (and `list(x)`, `x[:]`, `{**d}`) creates a new outer container whose elements are the same objects, so nested lists are shared. `copy.deepcopy` recursively copies, handling cycles with a memo dict. Deep copies are expensive; prefer immutable data or explicit construction where you can.

resources.title: Python docs — copy — Shallow and deep copy operations

cards.prompt: What does `if __name__ == "__main__":` do, and why use it?
cards.answer: A module's `__name__` is `"__main__"` only when it is run directly as a script; when imported it is the module's name. The guard runs code only in the first case, so the file can be both an importable module and a runnable script.
cards.explanation: Without it, importing the module (for tests, or by `multiprocessing` workers on Windows and macOS, which re-import the main module) re-runs the script's side effects. Keep the guarded block to a single `main()` call so the logic stays testable.

modules.name: Classes, Protocols & Exceptions
modules.description: Methods, properties, abstract bases, iteration protocols and exception design.

cards.prompt: `@classmethod` vs `@staticmethod`
cards.answer: A classmethod receives the class (`cls`) as its first argument; a staticmethod receives nothing implicit and is just a function namespaced in the class.

left.title: @classmethod
points: Polymorphic — sees the subclass it was called on
Can read and set class attributes

right.title: @staticmethod
points: A plain function grouped with the class
Cannot see the class or instance
Often better as a module function

cards.explanation: Classmethods respect subclassing: `Sub.from_json(...)` constructs a `Sub`, which is why alternative constructors are classmethods. If a staticmethod does not need the class at all, ask whether it should be a module-level function instead.

cards.prompt: A public `radius` attribute now needs validation, but hundreds of callers already use `circle.radius = 5`. How do you add the check without breaking them?
cards.answer: Turn it into a `@property` with a setter that validates. The attribute syntax stays identical for callers while the class regains control over reads and writes.
cards.explanation: This is why Python code does not start with Java-style getters and setters: plain attributes can be upgraded to properties later without any API change. Properties are descriptors under the hood; keep them cheap, because callers assume attribute access is fast.

cards.prompt: What is the difference between `__new__` and `__init__`?
cards.answer: `__new__` is a static method that creates and returns the instance; `__init__` initialises an instance that already exists and returns `None`. `__init__` only runs if `__new__` returns an instance of the class.
cards.explanation: You almost never need `__new__`. Its real uses are subclassing immutable types (`int`, `str`, `tuple` — their value is fixed before `__init__` could change it), instance caching, and metaclass work. Everything else belongs in `__init__`.

resources.title: Python docs — Data model — basic customisation

cards.prompt: `__repr__` vs `__str__`
cards.answer: `__repr__` is the unambiguous developer representation (shown in the REPL, debuggers and containers); `__str__` is the readable end-user form used by `print` and `str()`.
cards.explanation: If you implement only one, implement `__repr__` — `str()` falls back to it, and it is what appears when your object sits inside a list or a log line. Dataclasses generate a good `__repr__` automatically.

cards.prompt: `abc.ABC` vs `typing.Protocol`
cards.answer: An ABC is nominal — classes must inherit from it (or register) and abstract methods are enforced at instantiation. A Protocol is structural — any class with matching methods satisfies it, checked statically by the type checker.

left.title: ABC
points: Instantiating an incomplete subclass raises TypeError

right.title: Protocol
points: Checked by mypy/pyright, not at runtime
Works with classes you do not own

cards.explanation: Protocols are Python's formal duck typing: you can describe what an argument needs without forcing third-party classes to inherit anything, much like Go interfaces. Use an ABC when you want shared implementation and a runtime guarantee; a Protocol when you only want to describe a capability.

cards.prompt: What is the difference between an iterable and an iterator in Python?
cards.answer: An iterable has `__iter__` returning an iterator. An iterator has `__next__` (raising `StopIteration` when exhausted) and an `__iter__` that returns itself. Lists are iterables; `iter(list)` gives a fresh iterator each time.
cards.explanation: Iterators are single-pass: once exhausted they stay exhausted, which is why iterating a generator or a `map` object twice gives nothing the second time. `for` calls `iter()` then `next()` until `StopIteration`. Writing `__iter__` as a generator function is the easiest way to make a class iterable.

cards.prompt: How should you design custom exceptions for a library?
cards.answer: Define one base exception for the library (`class PaymentError(Exception)`) and specific subclasses beneath it (`CardDeclined`, `GatewayTimeout`). Inherit from `Exception`, never `BaseException`, and attach useful context as attributes.
cards.explanation: A common base lets callers catch "anything from this library" without catching unrelated bugs; specific subclasses let them handle the cases they care about. `BaseException` is reserved for `KeyboardInterrupt`, `SystemExit` and `GeneratorExit`, which should normally propagate.

resources.title: Python docs — Errors and exceptions — user-defined

cards.prompt: What is lost here, and how do you keep it?
cards.answer: Raising inside `except` without `from` still chains implicitly ("During handling… another exception occurred"), which reads like a second bug. Write `raise ConfigError(...) from err` to mark it as a deliberate translation and keep the original as `__cause__`.
cards.explanation: `raise X from err` sets `__cause__` and prints "The above exception was the direct cause of…". `raise X from None` suppresses the context when the original genuinely adds nothing. Never translate an exception without preserving the root cause — it is the most useful line in the traceback.

cards.prompt: What does this print?
cards.answer:
try
else
finally
done
cards.explanation: Order: the `try` body; `except` only on an exception; `else` only if no exception occurred; `finally` always, even after `return` or `break`. Putting code in `else` rather than at the end of `try` keeps the `except` from accidentally catching errors raised by that follow-up code.

cards.prompt: What is a descriptor, and which everyday features are built from them?
cards.answer: An object on a class that defines `__get__` (and optionally `__set__`/`__delete__`) to customise attribute access on instances. `property`, `classmethod`, `staticmethod`, bound methods, `__slots__` and ORM fields are all descriptors.
cards.explanation: Data descriptors (defining `__set__`) take priority over the instance `__dict__`; non-data descriptors (only `__get__`) are shadowed by it. Functions are non-data descriptors, and `__get__` is exactly how `obj.method` becomes a bound method carrying `self`.

cards.prompt: What does this print?
cards.code:
class Cart:
    items = []
    count = 0

a, b = Cart(), Cart()
a.items.append('milk')
b.items.append('eggs')
print(a.items, b.items)
Cart.count = 2
b.count = 1
print(a.count, b.count)
cards.answer:
['milk', 'eggs'] ['milk', 'eggs']
2 1
cards.explanation: `items = []` in the class body is a *class* attribute: one list shared by every instance, so both carts see both items. Mutable per-instance state belongs in `__init__` (`self.items = []`). Assigning through an instance (`b.count = 1`) instead creates an instance attribute that shadows the class one, which is why the counts differ.

resources.title: Python tutorial — Class and instance variables

modules.name: Standard Library, Packaging & Tooling
modules.description: Collections, itertools, pathlib, logging, asyncio, environments, packaging, imports and testing.

cards.prompt: What does this print?
cards.code:
from collections import Counter, defaultdict, deque
print(Counter('abracab').most_common(2))
g = defaultdict(list)
for k, v in [('x', 1), ('y', 3), ('x', 2)]:
    g[k].append(v)
print(dict(sorted(g.items())))
q = deque([1, 2])
q.appendleft(0)
print(list(q))
cards.explanation: `Counter` counts hashables and gives `most_common`; `defaultdict` creates missing values on first access, removing the "if key not in d" dance; `deque` gives O(1) appends and pops at both ends, where `list.pop(0)` is O(n). With `maxlen`, a deque becomes a bounded ring buffer.

cards.prompt: Which `itertools` functions are worth knowing by heart?
cards.answer: `chain` (concatenate iterables), `islice` (slice any iterator), `groupby` (group consecutive equal keys), `product`/`permutations`/`combinations` (combinatorics), `accumulate` (running totals), `batched` (fixed-size chunks, 3.12+), and `pairwise` (adjacent pairs, 3.10+).
cards.explanation: All are lazy, so they compose into memory-flat pipelines. The classic trap is `groupby`: it only groups *adjacent* equal keys, so sort by the same key first — exactly like `uniq` in the shell.

resources.title: Python docs — itertools — Functions creating iterators

cards.prompt: `pathlib.Path` vs `os.path` string handling
cards.answer: pathlib gives path objects with operators and methods; os.path treats paths as strings manipulated by functions.

right.title: os.path
points: Strings everywhere — easy to mix up
Still fine in old code, no reason for new code

cards.explanation: Always pass `encoding="utf-8"` when reading or writing text: the default depends on the platform locale, which makes the same code read files differently on Windows. PEP 686 makes UTF-8 the default in a future release for exactly this reason.

cards.prompt: What is wrong with this library code?
cards.code:
import logging
logging.basicConfig(level=logging.DEBUG)

def login(user_id):
    logging.info(f'user {user_id} logged in')
cards.answer: A library must never configure logging — `basicConfig` in an imported module hijacks the application's handlers and levels. Use `logger = logging.getLogger(__name__)` and let the application configure output. Also, pass arguments instead of an f-string.
cards.explanation: `logger.info("user %s logged in", user_id)` defers formatting until the record is actually emitted, and lets aggregators group messages by template. Use `logger.exception(...)` inside `except` to include the traceback. Named per-module loggers form a hierarchy the app can tune per package.

cards.prompt: What do `async def`, `await`, `asyncio.run` and `asyncio.gather` each do?
cards.answer: `async def` defines a coroutine function — calling it returns a coroutine object without running it. `await` suspends until the awaited thing finishes, yielding control to the event loop. `asyncio.run` starts a loop and runs a top-level coroutine. `gather` (or a `TaskGroup`) runs several concurrently and collects the results.
cards.explanation: Concurrency only happens when you schedule several tasks: awaiting coroutines one after another is still sequential. Prefer `async with asyncio.TaskGroup()` (3.11+), which cancels siblings when one fails, and use `asyncio.timeout()` to bound waits.

resources.title: Python docs — asyncio — Coroutines and tasks

cards.prompt: Two projects need different versions of the same library. How do you isolate them, and what should you never do?
cards.answer: Give each project its own virtual environment (`python -m venv .venv`, or a manager like `uv` or Poetry) and install into that. Never `sudo pip install` into the system interpreter — the OS itself depends on those packages.
cards.explanation: A venv is a directory with its own `site-packages` and a python link; activation just adjusts `PATH`. Record dependencies in `pyproject.toml` and pin exact versions in a lockfile for applications. Modern systems mark the system Python as "externally managed" (PEP 668) to block the mistake entirely.

resources.title: Python docs — venv — Creation of virtual environments

cards.prompt: What is `pyproject.toml`, and what replaced `setup.py`?
cards.answer: The standard project file: `[build-system]` names the build backend (hatchling, setuptools, poetry-core…), `[project]` holds metadata and dependencies (PEP 621), and `[tool.*]` tables configure tools such as ruff, mypy and pytest.
cards.explanation: Declarative metadata replaced executable `setup.py` scripts, so tools can read a project without running arbitrary code. Libraries declare compatible ranges (`requests>=2.31`); applications additionally pin exact versions in a lockfile for reproducible installs.

resources.title: Python Packaging User Guide — Writing pyproject.toml

cards.prompt: How does `import` find a module, and what happens on the second import?
cards.answer: Python searches `sys.path` — the script's directory, `PYTHONPATH`, then site-packages — for a module or package (a directory, usually with `__init__.py`). The module executes once and is cached in `sys.modules`; later imports return the cached object without re-running it.
cards.explanation: That caching is why module-level code runs only once and why circular imports can see a half-initialised module. Naming your script `random.py` or `json.py` shadows the standard library module — a classic confusing bug. Prefer absolute imports within a package.

cards.prompt: What does pytest give you over `unittest`, and what are fixtures?
cards.answer: Plain `assert` statements with rich failure introspection, test discovery by naming convention, parametrisation (`@pytest.mark.parametrize`), and fixtures — functions that provide setup to tests that name them as parameters, with `yield` for teardown and a configurable scope.
cards.explanation: Fixtures compose (one fixture can request another) and are injected by name, replacing inheritance-heavy `setUp` classes. Built-ins such as `tmp_path`, `monkeypatch` and `capsys` cover filesystem, environment and output capture without mocks.

cards.prompt: How do you type a function generically, and what are `TypedDict` and `Callable` for?
cards.answer: Python 3.12 syntax: `def first[T](xs: list[T]) -> T:` (older code uses `TypeVar`). `TypedDict` types dictionaries with known keys, such as JSON payloads. `Callable[[int, str], bool]` types functions passed as arguments.
cards.explanation: Annotations are not enforced at runtime — they are checked by mypy or pyright in CI. Validate untrusted data at the boundary with a runtime library such as Pydantic, then rely on static types inside. `Any` switches checking off; prefer `object` and narrow it.

resources.title: Python docs — typing — Support for type hints

cards.prompt: How does CPython free memory?
cards.answer: Primarily by reference counting: each object tracks how many references point at it and is freed the instant the count reaches zero. A generational cycle collector (`gc` module) periodically finds reference cycles that counting alone can never free.
cards.explanation: Deterministic refcounting is why `with open(...)` still matters but abandoned files usually close promptly in CPython — and why that is not guaranteed in PyPy. Objects in cycles with `__del__` used to be uncollectable; since 3.4 they are collected. `weakref` references an object without keeping it alive.

resources.title: Python docs — gc — Garbage Collector interface
